questions.prompt: An app uses the cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern. What happens when it reads a key that is not in the cache?

options: The cache notices the miss, loads the value from the database by itself, and returns it
The app reads the value from the database, returns it, and writes it into the cache
The database notices the miss and pushes the value into the cache for the app to read
The app returns an empty result and schedules a background job to warm the cache
payload.answer: The app reads the value from the database, returns it, and writes it into the cache

questions.explanation: In cache-aside the application owns the caching logic: on a miss it loads the value from the database itself and puts it in the cache, so later reads hit. A cache that loads missing values by itself is a different pattern, called read-through. The database does not know the cache exists, so it never pushes values into it. A miss is not an error and does not return empty data; it just costs one database read.

questions.prompt: Your app runs on one server. Traffic is expected to grow ten times over the next year, and the site must stay up if any single machine fails. Which approach meets both needs?

options: Move the app to the largest server that your cloud provider offers
Run the app on several servers and spread requests with a load balancer
Add a cache in front of the server so that each request costs less work
Configure the server to run more worker threads on the same machine
payload.answer: Run the app on several servers and spread requests with a load balancer

questions.explanation: Running copies of the app on several machines behind a load balancer is horizontal scaling (scaling out). You can keep adding machines as traffic grows, and if one machine dies the load balancer sends its traffic to the others. Moving to a bigger machine is vertical scaling (scaling up): there is a limit to how big a machine can get, and it is still one machine that can fail. A cache and more threads get more out of the one server, but if that server goes down, the whole site goes down with it.

questions.prompt: Your site is hosted in Virginia, and users in Australia say pages load slowly. Most of each page is images and script files that are the same for every user. How would a CDN (content delivery network) help most?

options: It would serve those files from servers close to the users in Australia
It would move your database to Australia so that its queries run faster
It would compress the files so they take less disk space on your server
It would take over your server's job, so the server could be switched off
payload.answer: It would serve those files from servers close to the users in Australia

questions.explanation: A CDN keeps copies of files that are the same for everyone on "edge" servers in many countries. An Australian user then fetches them from a nearby server instead of from Virginia, which removes most of the delay, because distance is what makes each request slow. A CDN does not move or speed up your database, and saving disk space on your server does not make files reach users any faster. Your own server (the origin) is still needed for anything the CDN has not cached yet and for pages that differ per user.

questions.prompt: A query that filters on one column is slow, so you add a database index on that column. What is the usual trade-off?

options: Both reads and writes get faster, because the rows are now kept in sorted order
Those reads get faster, but queries that filter on other columns get slower
Writes are unaffected; the only cost is the extra disk space the index uses
Those reads get faster, but inserts and updates must also update the index
payload.answer: Those reads get faster, but inserts and updates must also update the index

questions.explanation: An index lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table, like the index at the back of a book. The cost is that every insert, delete, and update to that column must also change the index, so writes do a little more work. The index does take disk space too, but that is not the only cost, and writes never get faster because of it. Queries on other columns are not slowed down; they simply do not use the new index.

questions.prompt: Why is an API easier to scale horizontally when its app servers are stateless?

options: Stateless servers keep each user's session in local memory, so lookups are faster
Any server can handle any request, so servers can be added or removed freely
Stateless servers do not need a database, so there is no shared bottleneck
Stateless servers use less memory, so each one can fit more concurrent users
payload.answer: Any server can handle any request, so servers can be added or removed freely

questions.explanation: A stateless server keeps nothing about a user between requests; session data lives in a shared store such as a database or cache, or in a signed token the client sends with each request. That means any server can answer any request, so new servers can join and old ones can leave without losing anyone's session. Keeping sessions in local memory is exactly what makes a server stateful. Stateless servers still use a database, and memory use is not the point.

questions.prompt: An order service calls an email service directly. During a sale the email service slows down, and orders start timing out. How does putting a message queue between them help?

options: The queue sends the emails itself, faster than the email service ever could
The queue guarantees each email lands in the customer's inbox exactly once
The queue lets the order service skip the email step when the email service is slow
Orders stop waiting on emails; the email service works through the backlog later
payload.answer: Orders stop waiting on emails; the email service works through the backlog later

questions.explanation: A queue decouples the two services. The order service drops an "email this customer" job on the queue and finishes the order straight away, so a slow email service no longer makes orders time out. A traffic spike becomes a backlog of jobs that the email service works through at its own pace. The queue does not send emails itself or make the email service faster. Queues do not promise exactly-once delivery, and nothing is skipped; each job waits in the queue until it is processed.

questions.prompt: A web app runs in California, but its database is in Europe. Each page runs 20 database queries, one after another, and takes over 3 seconds to load. The database says each query takes about 1 millisecond. What is the most effective fix?

options: Upgrade the database to a larger machine with faster disks
Move the app so it runs in the same region as the database
Add more app servers in California behind a load balancer
Add indexes to the columns that the queries filter on
payload.answer: Move the app so it runs in the same region as the database

questions.explanation: Each query has to travel across the Atlantic and back, which takes roughly 150 milliseconds. Twenty of those in a row add up to about 3 seconds, while the database's own work is only about 20 milliseconds in total. Running the app next to the database cuts each round trip to around a millisecond. A bigger database or new indexes would speed up the 1 millisecond of work, not the network wait. More app servers help when servers are overloaded, but every page would still wait on the same slow round trips. Sending the queries together in one batch would also help, because it pays for the round trip only once.

questions.prompt: A cache cluster picks the node for each key with hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of nodes. Before growing from 10 to 11 nodes, the team switches to consistent hashing. Which problem does this avoid?

options: Most keys would map to a different node, so most cache reads would suddenly miss
The new node would get no keys until every existing node had been restarted
Every key would be copied to every node, so memory use would grow with each node
The new node would receive most of the new keys and quickly become overloaded
payload.answer: Most keys would map to a different node, so most cache reads would suddenly miss

questions.explanation: Changing N from 10 to 11 changes hash(key) mod N for roughly 90% of keys. Each of those keys is now looked up on a node that does not have it, so almost the whole cache effectively empties at once and the database takes the full load. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring, so the new node takes over only its share (about 1 in 11 keys) and everything else stays put. Adding a node does not need restarts, and neither scheme copies every key to every node. Plain mod N spreads keys evenly across all nodes, so the new node is not overloaded; uneven spread is actually a weakness of basic consistent hashing, fixed with virtual nodes.

questions.prompt: A client sends a "charge $50" request, gets no response before its timeout, and retries. How should the payment API make sure the customer is charged only once?

options: The client sends a unique ID per charge; the server returns the saved result for repeats
Use HTTP POST for the charge, since the HTTP spec defines POST as an idempotent method
Tell clients not to retry after a timeout, and to show the user an error instead
Reject any charge that matches the same customer's amount from the last minute
payload.answer: The client sends a unique ID per charge; the server returns the saved result for repeats

questions.explanation: After a timeout the client cannot know whether the first charge went through, so retrying must be safe. If the client attaches a unique ID (an idempotency key) to each charge, the server can recognise a retry and return the original result instead of charging again. POST is not idempotent under the HTTP spec; GET, PUT and DELETE are. Not retrying leaves the user unsure whether they paid, and a charge that really failed is simply dropped. Blocking repeat amounts would wrongly reject a genuine second purchase.

questions.prompt: An API uses a token bucket rate limiter with a capacity of 10 tokens, refilled at 1 token per second. Each request uses one token, and a request that finds the bucket empty is rejected. A client has been idle for a minute, then sends 15 requests at once. What happens?

options: None are allowed, because the burst of 15 is larger than the capacity
Only 1 is allowed, because the refill rate is 1 token per second
10 are allowed straight away and the other 5 are rejected
All 15 are allowed, because the client built up 60 tokens while it was idle
payload.answer: 10 are allowed straight away and the other 5 are rejected

questions.explanation: Tokens build up while the client is idle, but never beyond the bucket's capacity, so the bucket holds 10 tokens, not 60. The first 10 requests each take a token and succeed; the last 5 find the bucket empty and are rejected. This is the point of a token bucket: it allows short bursts up to the capacity while holding the long-run rate to the refill rate. It does not limit every second to 1 request, and it does not reject the whole burst.

questions.prompt: A very popular cache entry expires. In the same instant thousands of requests miss the cache and all query the database for that one value, overloading it. Which fix targets this problem most directly?

options: Shorten the entry's expiry time (TTL) so the value is refreshed much more often
Switch the cache's eviction policy from LRU to LFU so popular keys are kept
Add more cache nodes, so the load for the popular key is spread across machines
Let a single request recompute the value while the others wait or get the old one
payload.answer: Let a single request recompute the value while the others wait or get the old one

questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede (also called a thundering herd). The fix is to make sure only one request rebuilds the value, using a lock, while the rest wait for it or are served the slightly stale copy. Refreshing a little before expiry, at a random moment, is a related fix. A shorter expiry time makes expiries happen more often, so it makes things worse. The eviction policy (LRU or LFU) decides what is removed when memory is full, not what happens when an entry expires. More cache nodes do not help, because every request misses at the same moment and goes to the database anyway.

questions.prompt: An events table is split across 30 database servers (shards) by date, and each shard holds one day of events. Writing new events is slow, and adding more shards has not helped. What is the most likely cause?

options: All new events go to today's shard, so one server handles nearly all the writes
Each extra shard adds a fixed cost to every write, so 30 shards is simply too many
Every write must be copied to all 30 shards to keep the shards consistent
Each write must first check all 30 shards to find the one it belongs to
payload.answer: All new events go to today's shard, so one server handles nearly all the writes

questions.explanation: Sharding by date sends every new write to the newest shard, creating a hot spot: there are 30 servers, but only one is doing the write work, which is why adding shards changes nothing. The usual fix is to shard by something spread evenly, such as a hash of the user or event ID, at the cost of time-range queries having to read several shards. Shards do not add a per-shard cost to each write, a write goes to one shard rather than all of them, and the date alone tells the system which shard to use, so no search is needed.

questions.prompt: A service goes down for a minute. Its 500 clients each retry a failed call exactly 1 second later, again and again. When the service comes back, the flood of retries knocks it over again, and this repeats. Which change to the clients best breaks this cycle?

options: Retry straight away instead, so that no request spends time sitting idle
Make each call's timeout longer, raising it from 2 seconds to 10 seconds
Wait longer after each failure, plus a random extra delay per client
Send each retry to the service twice, in case one copy gets lost
payload.answer: Wait longer after each failure, plus a random extra delay per client

questions.explanation: The retries are in sync: all 500 clients fire at the same moments, so the recovering service is hit by all of them at once (a retry storm). Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure (1 s, 2 s, 4 s and so on), which cuts the total load. Jitter adds a random amount to each wait, so the clients spread out instead of arriving together. Retrying straight away or sending duplicates adds even more load. A longer timeout changes how long each client waits for an answer, not how many requests hit the service at once. A circuit breaker, which stops calling a failing service for a while, is a related fix.

questions.prompt: A newest-first feed API pages with LIMIT 20 OFFSET n, and new posts are added to the top all the time. Users paging down see repeated posts. What is the usual fix?

options: Raise the page size to 100, so users need fewer pages and run into fewer repeats
Add an index on the post timestamp, so that each page query runs faster
Sort the posts again on the client, so they always display in a stable order
Switch to cursor pagination: fetch the 20 posts older than the last one seen
payload.answer: Switch to cursor pagination: fetch the 20 posts older than the last one seen

questions.explanation: With offsets, every new post at the top pushes older posts down, so the next page's offset lands on items the user already saw. A cursor anchors the next page to the last item returned (for example its timestamp plus ID), so new posts above it do not shift anything. It is also faster on deep pages, because the database does not have to count past all the skipped rows. Bigger pages only make repeats rarer, an index only speeds up the query, and sorting on the client cannot remove duplicates that the server sent.

questions.prompt: A database is replicated across two data centers. The network link between them fails, but clients on both sides keep sending reads and writes. What choice does the CAP theorem say the system faces?

options: Give up partition tolerance, since CAP lets you pick any two of the three properties
None: with synchronous replication it can stay both consistent and available
Trade lower latency against higher throughput until the link is restored
Stay available and let the two sides diverge, or stay consistent and refuse some requests
payload.answer: Stay available and let the two sides diverge, or stay consistent and refuse some requests

questions.explanation: CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between staying consistent (refusing requests that could return stale or conflicting data) and staying available (answering anyway and reconciling later). A broken link is not something you can opt out of, so "pick any two" by dropping partition tolerance is a common misreading. Synchronous replication cannot complete across a broken link, so writes block, which gives up availability. Latency versus throughput is not the CAP trade-off; the related PACELC model adds that, even without a partition, systems trade latency against consistency.

questions.prompt: A key-value store keeps 3 copies (replicas) of every key. A write succeeds once W replicas confirm it, and a read asks R replicas and keeps the newest value. You need every read to see the latest successful write, and writes must keep working when one replica is down. Which setting meets both needs?
questions.explanation: A read is guaranteed to reach at least one replica holding the latest write when R + W is greater than the number of replicas (3). W = 2, R = 2 gives 4, so any 2 replicas you read must include one of the 2 that confirmed the write, and with one replica down there are still 2 left to confirm writes and 2 to answer reads. W = 3, R = 1 also overlaps (3 + 1 = 4), but every write needs all 3 replicas, so a single failure stops writes. W = 1, R = 2 and W = 2, R = 1 add up to only 3, so a read can land entirely on replicas that missed the latest write. Overlap alone is not full linearizability; concurrent writes and "sloppy" quorums that borrow other nodes need extra care.

questions.prompt: Producers add 1,000 jobs per second to an in-memory queue with no size limit. Workers can finish only 800 per second. This lasts for hours, and adding workers is not possible right now. What is the sound fix?

options: Move the queue to a machine with much more memory so it can hold the backlog
Keep the queue on disk instead of in memory, so it can hold far more jobs
Limit the queue's size, and reject or slow down producers when it is full
Put jobs that have waited too long back on the queue so they are retried
payload.answer: Limit the queue's size, and reject or slow down producers when it is full

questions.explanation: When jobs arrive faster than they can be finished, the queue grows by 200 jobs every second (720,000 an hour) and every job waits longer than the one before. More memory or a disk-backed queue only delays the crash while wait times keep climbing; a queue can absorb short bursts, not a lasting gap. Back-pressure fixes this: cap the queue, and when it is full make producers block, back off, or get a "try again later" error, so the overload is visible and the system stays healthy. Re-adding old jobs puts even more work into a queue that is already too long. The long-term fix is more worker capacity or less incoming work.

questions.prompt: When an order is saved, the service must also publish an OrderCreated event to a message broker. The code commits the database transaction, then publishes. If the process crashes between those two steps, the order is saved but the event is never sent. Which design prevents this?

options: Publish the event first, and commit the database transaction after that
Save the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; publish it from there
Wrap the publish in a try/catch block that retries it until the broker accepts it
Have the broker confirm each event before the order request returns
payload.answer: Save the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; publish it from there

questions.explanation: The commit and the publish are two separate operations with no shared transaction, so a crash between them loses the event. The transactional outbox fixes this: the event is written to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order, so both exist or neither does. A separate process then reads the outbox and publishes each event, retrying until it succeeds (so consumers must cope with the occasional duplicate). Publishing first just flips the failure into an event for an order that was never saved. A try/catch retry and a broker confirmation both run inside the process, so they do nothing if the process crashes before publishing.

questions.prompt: Each user request fans out to 100 backend servers in parallel and must wait for all of them. Each server answers slowly 1% of the time, independently of the others. Roughly what share of user requests will be slow?

options: About 1%
About 10%
About 63%
About 99%
payload.answer: About 63%

questions.explanation: A user request is fast only if all 100 responses are fast: 0.99^100 is about 0.37, so about 63% of requests hit at least one slow server. This is why systems that fan out watch p99 and p99.9 latency rather than averages, and use techniques such as hedged requests (sending a backup request if the first is slow) to cut the tail. The 1% answer ignores the fan-out, and 99% comes from adding 1% a hundred times, which overcounts because the chances of independent events do not simply add up.

questions.prompt: A user changes their display name. The write goes to the primary database, but the next page load reads from an asynchronously updated read replica and shows the old name. Which approach fixes this for that user without sending everyone's reads to the primary?

options: Send that user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write
Add more read replicas, so each one has less work and applies changes sooner
Put a cache in front of the replica, so the name is served from memory instead
Set the replica's isolation level to read committed, so it skips stale rows
payload.answer: Send that user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write

questions.explanation: This is replication lag breaking read-your-writes consistency: the replica has not applied the change yet. A common fix is to route a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or until the replica has caught up to that write, while everyone else keeps using replicas. More replicas do not reduce lag and add work for the primary, which has to feed each of them. A cache in front of the replica can hold the stale value even longer. Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions see on one database; they cannot make a replica return a change it has not received yet.
